#1339. Late Benjamin Goal Secures Deserved Point For Under-21s

A superb late equaliser from Omari Benjamin secured a deserved 1-1 draw for Everton's Under-21s away at Crystal Palace in Premier League 2.

Benjamin's turn past the last man and chipped finish ensured a share of the spoils for Dave Hughes' side, who had gone behind to Seb Williams' goal early in the second half but always looked threatening and could have won it late on.

Academy graduate Tom Davies also featured for the Under-21s, coming on as a second-half substitute as the Academy continues to support the midfielder with his fitness while he looks to secure a professional contract elsewhere.

Four changes were made from the side that defeated Tamworth 3-2 in the National League Cup in midweek. Ezra Carrington returned to the starting XI at left-back with Melvin Matos slotting into central midfield, while Under-18s players John Dodds and Harry Brookes were both given starts in central defence and attacking midfield respectively.

Chances were at somewhat of a premium in the early stages although the Toffees were working the ball nicely in possession. In the 10th minute Brookes burst into the box after striker Ceiran Loney won possession back in the final third, but as he fired at goal Brookes saw his effort blocked by a last-ditch sliding challenge from Palace captain George King.

The danger man for Palace looked to be Dean Benamar and the winger twice sent efforts at goal in the first half, drilling one effort narrowly wide in the 18th minute before forcing a fine stop from Toffees keeper Fraser Barnsley eight minutes later.

Everton responded well with Braiden Graham curling one effort high and wide from 18 yards and skipper Will Tamen heading narrowly wide from a corner on the stroke of half-time, while Palace rattled the crossbar through Amaari Sealey's effort.

The period immediately after the restart gave a hint as to how the second half would play out. Palace immediately got on the attack but could not find a way to goal, and the Toffees countered superbly as a result, with Loney being played through one-on-one only for keeper Lucca Benetton to produce an excellent stop to deny the Scottish youth international.

That lifted Palace and shortly after he had seen a flicked effort from eight yards fly wide of the far post, Williams made no mistake with his second effort just past the hour, poking the ball past Barnsley after King's flick-on into the box split the defence.

King would then rattle the woodwork five minutes later as Palace looked for a second goal, but the Toffees defended manfully and gradually began to take control of the game. Substitute Jonathan Nsangou thought he had won a penalty in the 77th minute when he was brought down after surging into the box from the right channel, but the referee gave a free kick on the edge and Benjamin headed wide from Graham's delivery.

But there was still time for an equaliser and it duly came with five minutes of regular time to play. Luis Gardner stepped out from centre-back and played an arrowed forward pass to Benjamin, who flicked the ball with the outside of his foot around King before racing onto it and into the box.

King and Benetton both tried to challenge the Everton man but it was no use – Benjamin dinked the ball eloquently over the on-rushing goalkeeper and it nestled in the back of the net.

If either side was going to win it late on, it looked more likely to be the Toffees, who sent a series of deliveries into the box but could not find that final shot on goal, and the points were shared in South London.

Speaking after the game, Head of Academy Player Development Dave Hughes told evertonfc.com: "We felt (we deserved a point at least). We had probably four or five really good chances with counters in the final third, and maybe didn’t get our shots away cleanly. They got some excellent blocks in and around the box.

"We definitely felt we didn’t deserve to lose and I'm sure they’d say similar. For the first 15-20 minutes we controlled large parts of the game, in the second half it became more open. We showed great character and resilience to stay in the game after going 1-0 down and that’s one thing you’d give the lads credit for – in every game, if we’ve gone behind, we’ve found a way to get back into it. We had a good spell at the end where we maybe could have finished it.

"It's a great finish from Omari, outstanding actually, over the keeper, and the turn as well.

"It's pleasing to have got so many of the Under-18s on. John Dodds started, Malik and Jonathan Nsangou came on, Harry Brookes played – all-in-all it's a very good afternoon. A result we definitely warranted and plenty of positives to take. It was great to see Will Tamen step up his time again from Tuesday night as well, we're really pleased for him.

"We're pleased with how the group are going about their work. Performances have been consistent and I feel as though the lads are giving a good account of themselves. We’ve been difficult to play against at times, but of course we can be more so.

"Tom’s an unbelievable professional. All the staff and players have witnessed that he’s a model professional in the way that he goes about his work. He’s shown the players, if they needed it, what a top professional looks like. How he trains, how he conducts himself. He’s given guidance and advice to the younger players. He’s been a credit to himself and to the Academy."

Liverpool are reportedly preparing for the possibility of life after Alisson Becker, with Porto goalkeeper Diogo Costa emerging as a serious target for 2027.

Alisson’s contract expires next summer, and uncertainty over a renewal has forced Liverpool to think carefully about the next phase of their goalkeeping plans.

Giorgi Mamardashvili is already at the club, while Lucca Brughmans and Armin Pecsi are highly rated internally, but there are doubts over whether any of them are ready to immediately replace one of the best goalkeepers of Liverpool’s modern era.

According to Anfield Watch, Liverpool have identified Diogo Costa as a leading option if Alisson leaves when his deal expires.

The report claims Liverpool admire Costa’s experience, shot-stopping and ability with the ball at his feet, qualities that would fit naturally into Andoni Iraola’s system.

Liverpool are not completely convinced that Mamardashvili is ready to become the undisputed No.1, while Brughmans is still considered one for the future. Pecsi is also viewed as part of a longer-term plan and could be sent out on loan again next season.

Liverpool’s interest in Costa is not entirely new either. CaughtOffside reported earlier this year that the Reds had already been tracking the Portugal international as a potential Alisson successor.

From Liverpool’s perspective, Costa would be a logical replacement.

He is already experienced at Champions League and international level, is comfortable playing out from the back and would arrive ready to compete immediately rather than needing a long adaptation period.

The uncertainty around Alisson has also increased. Iraola admitted this week that he does not know whether the Brazilian will stay, although he made clear that he would like him to continue at Anfield.

That makes succession planning essential rather than premature.

Liverpool could simply promote Mamardashvili, but replacing Alisson with an established goalkeeper such as Costa would reduce the risk of a major drop-off in such a crucial position.

The challenge will be price. Porto have never been an easy club to negotiate with, and Costa remains one of their most valuable players.

Still, if Alisson does leave in 2027, Liverpool will need quality rather than compromise. Costa looks like one of the strongest options available.

#1337. Kane’s record-equalling cap was no different to his first

The 125th cap was no different to the first for Harry Kane, who has now been in the business of goal accumulation for so long that it is only at the landmark moments, that all of us are obliged to step back and take in the full scale of the work he has created.

Peter Shilton took 20 years to rack up his 125 caps, while for Kane it has been just 11 – and then there are the goals. Two more on Tuesday took him to 91 which means that only 12 other England players in history have more England caps than Kane has England goals. This unassuming man from Chingford, who looks like a mildly rebellious academic from the late 1950s, was at it again: the first-time strike, the back-post header. He has some misses across these 11 years, most infamously from the penalty spot against France at the Qatar World Cup almost four years ago, so, yes, there are some regrets too. But what sticks is the way he has taken his chances – again and again.

ONE-TOUCH BRILLIANCE! ✨ Anderson, Rogers and Kane combine beautifully to double England's lead 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿 Cap No. 125, goal No. 90 for the skipper 👏 https://t.co/otMcxlXyps

Following his debut goal in 2015 against Lithuania, Kane has missed just 27 of the 152 England games since. He has added to the total like a great Test batsman patiently moving the scoreboard along. There was a bad run without goals in 2020 and before that in 2018. He scored only five in his first 17 caps and then scored 14 in his next 10. Against a very mediocre Czech Republic team this was classic late-era Kane, picking his moments and taking those chances with the usual absence of nerves. He was even substituted before the end.

Hall ➡️ Kane! The Newcastle fullback swings in the corner and it's the England captain who rises highest to head home 💥 https://t.co/5EhAcNZUqm

Afterwards at a Wembley press conference to mark the occasion, he invoked the cricket analogy himself on the question of scoring 100 England goals. “Being in the 90s, I try not to think about it too much, and it’s like I guess being a cricketer in the 90s. The more you think about the hundred… you don’t always get there.” There has still not been the elusive major trophy in the Kane England years but there has been success relative to the three decades that came before it. Semi-finals, finals – a good team if not a winning team.

At the centre of it has been a man around whom there has never been any scandal or, by the usual measure, much that might be described as spectacular. Rather it has been the scope of Kane’s career that is the most striking. The volume of the goals, of appearances, the capacity to be available – to play, to score – and the absolute quality of the player himself. He is determined to wring the very last drop out of his talent and usually refuses to acknowledge the prospect of the end, although there was a nod to it this time. “At some stage you know this opportunity isn’t going to be here,” he said. “I’m not going to be around forever, and I still hope that’s a long way away. But ultimately, of course, there’s times you’re tired or you’re injured, but I know I’ll miss it when it’s done. I try to always remind myself that and always try to make myself available.”

One expects that when the end comes it will not be as rancorous as the final exit of Cristiano Ronaldo from Portugal, a drama playing out elsewhere. At some point, Kane will take his leave and it is likely to be as unassuming as the rest of it. He will be back at Wembley, injury permitting, for cap No 126 next month against Croatia. He talks like a different person to the one he was even five years ago – with a confidence and certainty about his place in the world. As opposed to the younger Kane, who seemed to regard everything outside his goalscoring tunnel vision with a general sense of bemusement.

“Availability,” he said, “is one of the biggest strengths you can have at this level for any coach.” He was keen to emphasise his “all-round leadership” too, “a lot of assets off the pitch”. He still measures himself in goals, of course, and perhaps there will be a Ballon d’Or too later this month – a prize that has eluded generations of England players before him who have won much more for their clubs than Kane has done. The good news for Kane is that his last England years will be spent in a very good England team – one which was on another level to its opposition on this occasion too.

No team in the top tier of the Nations League has scored more goals than England – 14 in the last four match days. Tuchel’s name was sung at Wembley and even if the World Cup semi-final collapse in Atlanta in July has not been entirely forgotten, the roughest edges have been taken off somewhat. Another great performance from Jude Bellingham and also from Morgan Rogers, in place of Bukayo Saka. Another dominant Elliot Anderson performance in midfield. They left Wembley to applause and a sense of optimism renewed.

England kept the ball with such authority, and none more so than Bellingham. Trent Alexander-Arnold came back at right-back. Myles Lewis-Skelly returned for another bite at a Wembley midfield job. As in Prague last week, there was a self-inflicted Czech calamity in the first half. The captain Vladimir Coufal appeared to lose his cool at the threat of the England attack all over the Czechs’ half. No other reason for this Premier League experienced full-back to fling himself at Kane’s cross and drill the ball past Newcastle goalkeeper Lukas Hornicek on 27 minutes.

The second goal, on 40 minutes, was one for the ages. Anderson’s ball out to the right was met first time by Rogers for the cross and Kane ran into the space, as he has done so many times, to deliver a finish struck with customary assuredness. Bellingham almost flicked in Rogers’s cross on 56 minutes and from the corner that came after, Kane nodded in a header at the back post from Lewis Hall’s cross. All said, the defending was woeful but there was nothing wrong with the finish.

Thomas Tuchel believes England have taken a step forward from their World Cup heartbreak over this international break and said he was “honoured” to hear fans sing his name.

England finished their four Nations League games with a 3-0 win over Czech Republic, in which Harry Kane scored twice on his record-equalling 125th appearance.

It meant that Tuchel’s team have won three and lost one, against Spain, of their four games since the World Cup, after which the England head coach was heavily criticised for the semi-final defeat to Argentina.

Tuchel seems to have won the forgiveness of some England supporters, who sang his name at the start and the end of Tuesday’s game.

“It means a lot,” Tuchel said. “It’s amazing to have a song. It’s the biggest honour. And I’m very happy and very honoured. They can be sure that I will give my absolute best to make our team win and play well.”

Asked if he sensed a change in mood around his England team since the fall-out from the World Cup, Tuchel said: “I do and I think it’s necessary to move on. I think I can only repeat that we didn’t go out in the group stage. Sometimes it feels like that and we didn’t. As I said, our aim was always to progress, move forward and improve.”

Tuchel snapped back at a reporter who questioned why he felt it necessary to repeat that England had not gone out in the group stage of the World Cup, claiming the criticism had felt a “little bit” too harsh.

But on whether England have shown they are a step ahead of where the team were at the World Cup during this international camp, Tuchel was far more positive and replied: “Of course and that’s what we have to do. That is our goal to constantly improve and develop.

“We had these experiences together and we had a big tournament together, and it was very positive. It’s necessary to move forward and improve, especially in sports. This is what we’re trying to do.

“We adjusted some details in our structure and we didn’t compromise on the effort and the intensity, and on the togetherness of the team. The players who were with us in the World Cup took care of these standards and of the culture within the team, off the pitch and on the pitch, and I think that’s what you could see.”

We played a very good match, very fluid and to put it into context it was the fourth match in 11 or 12 days. We dominated the whole match, had some good opportunities, scored some beautiful goals. Subs were strong. Very good performance again.

[Leading the way, Mr Kane] Of course. That’s what he does. I don’t take it for granted. It’s just exceptional, every single match. It’s just difficult to find new words to express it.

Training, attitude, cohesion, belief, of course [is why they’re stronger than ever].

[Has the World Cup made England stronger?]  Of course, we got the first medal in 60 years. We didn’t go out in the group stage. We had a strong qualification, strong World Cup and strong camp. All four matches were on a high level. The camp throughout from the first day was on the highest level. You learn every day together. We grew stronger.

I was happy that everyone who was in the camp was contributing. Everyone was on the pitch. Everyone showed he was willing to give everything for the team and for the shirt. The guys who were with us for the World Cup set the standards high, made everyone feel welcome and everyone had a good camp.

He’s the best England player evert to wear the shirt and it’s an honour to play with him. And he’s only getting better.

A perfect night for me personally and also for the team. It’s been a tough camp, a long camp with some difficult games so it’s nice to finish it off all together. An extremely proud evening for me.

You saw some fantastic football out there tonight. The way we’re moving, the one-touch stuff, a fantastic ball from Elliot to Morgan and then a first time cross which was as good as it gets. As a striker you’re just waiting for those opportunities.

It started in the first game [reaching a higher level] although the result didn’t go for us. First game after a tournament, obviously this was a four-game camp, we had to find it [a higher level] and find it quickly. That’s the most pleasing thing.

This is the England team. There’s always going to be competition for places. It’s about taking the opportunity whether it’s 90 minutes, five minutes, whatever it was, make the most of it. You’re seeing that, everyone wants to be part of this. That’s only going to make us better for sure.

[Now for cap 126 next month?] That would be nice for sure.

Because places between teams who finish on the same points in the first instance are decided on head-to-heads, Croatia will have to beat England 8-0 at Wembley next month to have any hope of stopping them from qualifying for the quarter-finals.

Having [four games and two weeks’ training] for patterns is very good. It’s a different style of play from the clubs. If you have more than two games you can have a training session, show, debrief and let the patterns sink in.

England conclude the group stage with matches against Croatia at Wembley on Nov 12 and at Madrid’s Metropolitano on Nov 15. They have to finish second to make it into the knockout rounds.

Which means they have bumped Emmerdale Farm off the schedule. Shame. I was looking forward to catching up with Amos Brearley and Mr Wilkes after all these years.

Hornicek; Coufal, Hranac, Vitik, Slama: Kral, Sadilek; Ambros, Sulc, Lingr; Naderi.

Sulc, who was sent off in Prague, returns after serving his ban in the defeat by Spain. From the starters in Prague, there are changes in goal, right-back, left centre-back, one midfield pivot both wingers and centre-forward with Kovar discarded for Newcastle’s Hornicek, the former Hammer Coufal returning as captain in place of Chaloupek, Bologna’s Vitik in for Wolves’ Krejci, Cerv stands down for Copenhagen’s Kral, Naderi of Rangers replaces Hlozek, Lingr of The Cranberries puts Radosta on the bench while Anderlecht’s Ambros takes over from Radosta.

Out go Konsa, Scott, Saka and Gordon for Alexander-Arnold, Lewis-Skelly, Rogers and Eze.

Your #ThreeLions to take on Czechia! ✨ https://t.co/JZ5kSYF1In

Harry Kane is scheduled to hold a press conference after the match at Wembley to talk about the achievement of joining Peter Shilton on 125 caps.

Secret to Harry Kane’s England longevity? ‘He strikes the ball better than Ronaldo’

Right foot, goal. Left foot, goal. Edge of the area, goal. Inside the area, goal. Under pressure, goal, Right foot, save. Left foot, goal. That was Harry Kane’s warm-up prior to England’s 7-0 demolition of Croatia and it underlined just why the striker will equal Peter Shilton’s appearance record on Tuesday night.

As demonstrated in Rijeka, Kane’s career has been a non-stop pursuit of excellence that has led him to the very top of the national game. England’s record goalscorer will also become the joint most-capped player with Shilton, when he makes his 125th appearance against the Czech Republic at Wembley on Tuesday night.

Eberechi Eze is set to start for England in the clash against Czech Republic tonight. The Arsenal forward is poised to come in for Anthony Gordon, who has started in the three matches during the Nations League international break. Trent Alexander-Arnold is also due to play at right-back, with Jarell Quansah moving to centre-back to cover for Ezri Konsa.

Alex Scott has been ruled out through injury, which has upset Bournemouth after he played in the win over Croatia at the weekend. Myles Lewis-Skelly is expected to get a recall to the team after playing against Czech Republic in Prague last week when England won 2-0. Morgan Rogers, who scored against Croatia, is in line to start in place of Bukayo Saka.

Probable England team: Pickford; Trent, Quansah, Guehi, Hall; Lewis-Skelly, Anderson; Rogers, Bellingham, Eze; Kane

Advertisement | GambleAware | 18+ Betting on the football tonight? Take a look at these tips and offers chosen by Telegraph Media Group

Good evening and welcome to live coverage of England vs Czech Republic from Wembley in the fourth and mercifully final round of fixtures in this sprawling Nations League international break. Tonight Harry Kane will win his 125th cap and equal Peter Shilton for England appearances.

Shilton’s took him 20 years as Gordon Banks was simply too good in the couple of years following his debut and then a couple of managers, Don Revie and Ron Greenwood, preferred Ray Clemence until the latter finally plumped for Shilton as No 1 in 1979. Kane’s, by contrast, have taken him 11. In that time he has been rested for a handful of friendlies but has not been unused in a competitive match when fit since Gareth Southgate left him out of the 5-0 victory over Sam Marino in 2021’s World Cup qualifier when Dominic Calvert-Lewin scored two and Ollie Watkins one goal on his debut.

England played the Czech Republic a week ago, winning 2-0 in Prague by virtue of Anthony Gordon’s cute header and Kane’s clever shot through a defender’s legs but they huffed and puffed for ages against a team harshly reduced to 10 men until they blew the house down. They went on to marmalise Croatia 7-0 in their next game in front of a crowd that sounded like a cross between the choirs on Another Brick in the Wall, Part 2 and There’s No One Quite Like Grandma.

In the past England have had problems backing up their best performances – the 4-1 evisceration of the Dutch at Euro 96 was followed by the cagey display in the quarter-final against Spain before prevailing on penalties, the 5-1 victory in Munich in 2001 led to a drab 2-0 win against Albania at St James’ Park the following Tuesday, in 2016 they went to Berlin and beat world champions Germany but were thumped by Netherlands, who had not even qualified for Euro 2016, a couple of days later. Even their thrilling, second-half showing against Croatia in their World Cup opener in June preceded the dreary 0-0 draw with Ghana.

Given the attacking fluency in Rijeka, Thomas Tuchel must be tempted not to to ring the changes and replace seven or eight players. He will have to find replacements for the injured Alex Scott and Ezri Konsa, however, and Calvert Lewin, who has had seven minutes of action, Rio Ngumoha 19, Morgan Gibbs-White 27 and Jarrad Branthwaite one, may feel they deserve a fairer opportunity to show what they can do in a match.

#1336. Michael Carrick reveals club bosses have not told him if he will still have a job next week, with Man United languishing in relegation zone ahead of Aston Villa clash

Published: 17:30 EDT, 7 November 2026 | Updated: 04:50 EDT, 8 November 2026

Michael Carrick has not been given any guarantees over his future beyond Sunday's game against Aston Villa at Old Trafford as Manchester United dropped into the relegation zone.

United bosses handed Carrick more time to turn the club's season around following the 3-0 defeat to Bournemouth a fortnight ago amid speculation he could be replaced by Eddie Howe or Julian Nagelsmann.

In the two games since then, Carrick's side have lost at Chelsea and staged a rousing comeback over Roma in the Champions League to secure a first win in 10 games.

United slipped into the bottom three after Nottingham Forest beat Manchester City on Saturday, and could be in last place by the time they kick off against Villa depending on the outcome of other games involving Sunderland and Crystal Palace on Sunday.

The situation could leave Carrick's position under threat during the two-week international break. Asked if he has been told outright that he will be in charge next week, the United boss replied: 'No. Just carry on as absolute normal.

'Whatever is going to happen is going to happen. I'm really looking forward to the next game, playing at home on the back of the other night.

Michael Carrick revealed that club chiefs have not told him if he'll be in charge next week

Sir Jim Ratcliffe (left), Omar Berrada (centre) and Jason Wilcox (right) have not informed their manager about their plans for the international break

'The supporters are hopefully looking forward to coming energised and feeling good about what they might see, and we've got to repay that.'

Carrick is preparing for a normal international break, and doesn't have any plans to spend more time with his family after a turbulent period at Old Trafford.

'Not really different to normal. Genuinely not,' he added. 'I think international breaks are always a time to re-energise and freshen up. Some of the players that go away to internationals get freshened up in a different environment, but I don't really need it. I'm fine as I am.

'We'll certainly train next week and maybe have the weekend off. We'll see how that develops, who's left behind, who's with us and what they need.'

Carrick insisted that he and Bruno Fernandes have put any issues behind them after the United captain criticised his tactics in the Champions League defeat to Como last month.

After he led United's fightback against Roma in midweek by converting a twice taken penalty, Fernandes confirmed that Carrick's decision to drop him for the Bournemouth game was due to a loss of form, and disputed that the two men had a clear-the-air meeting over his comments.

But Carrick said: 'There are always conversations, bits going on; acknowledging certain things of when things are going well, what we need to improve on as a group.

'Sometimes it's individually, sometimes it's group. We always have discussions. What's actually said in that discussion, I'll keep that to myself.

'But I think it's pretty clear we've moved in a good direction, and Bruno's commitment is undoubted for me (in terms) of what he brings to this team and this club.

'He showed that again this week by his actions, the way he's played and how he dealt with even retaking the penalty and the frame of mind he was in for that. I think that tells you everything. Bruno's as good as ever.'

Alisson Becker could be heading towards the end of his Liverpool career, with Fabrizio Romano revealing there is now a serious possibility the Brazilian leaves Anfield when his contract expires next summer.

The 34-year-old has been one of Liverpool’s most important players since arriving from Roma in 2018, but his current deal only runs until June 2027.

With no active renewal talks taking place, the Reds may soon face one of their biggest succession decisions in years.

Speaking on his YouTube channel, Romano explained that Liverpool were aware Alisson considered a move to Juventus earlier in 2026 before deciding to stay for another season.

Romano said Liverpool activated a one-year extension because the club were already going through major changes, with Mohamed Salah, Andy Robertson and other senior figures departing.

Alisson ultimately chose to remain and help during the transition from Arne Slot to Andoni Iraola, but Romano now believes a summer exit is realistic.

“I think it’s a serious possibility,” Romano said when discussing whether this could be Alisson’s final Liverpool season.

Iraola himself has admitted he does not know whether Alisson will stay, although he made clear that he hopes the goalkeeper signs a new deal.

Losing Alisson for nothing would be a huge moment for Liverpool.

Even at 34, he remains one of the defining goalkeepers of his generation and replacing his shot-stopping, distribution and leadership would not be straightforward.

Liverpool are already preparing for that possibility. Aston Villa goalkeeper Zion Suzuki is being monitored as a potential long-term successor.

Giorgi Mamardashvili is another option already at Anfield, while Liverpool have also been linked with Porto goalkeeper Diogo Costa.

The interesting part is that an Alisson exit is not yet inevitable. Romano stressed that Liverpool could still offer him a new contract if their stance changes.

That decision should not be delayed too long. Allowing one of Liverpool’s greatest modern players to leave without having a clear replacement ready would be a major gamble.

For now, Alisson’s future remains unresolved, but the possibility of a summer farewell feels more realistic than ever.

#1334. Replacing the neurons that Parkinson’s destroys

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Laura Dattaro is a science journalist in Maplewood, New Jersey.

In people with Parkinson’s disease, neurons in the brain that produce dopamine are continuously lost. Without the neurotransmitter, which is crucial for movement, control of motor function begins to break down, resulting in symptoms such as tremors — one of the hallmarks of Parkinson’s.

Replacing dopamine is the goal of many treatments. Since the 1960s, that’s been done with a drug called levodopa, an amino acid that the brain converts to dopamine. But that conversion is carried out by the dopamine neurons that Parkinson’s eats away at. Lose too many, and the medication can no longer reliably control symptoms.

Some researchers have therefore long been eyeing the possibility of restoring those neurons. That entails growing them outside the brain and then injecting them through holes drilled into each side of the skull. The hope is that the cells will take root and begin to replenish the dwindling supply of dopamine.

Nearly four decades after such a transplant was first attempted, the work is beginning to pay off. Since early 2025, four phase I and II clinical trials have reported early results showing that the treatment is largely safe, with some people reporting improved motor skills and less ‘off’ time, during which their medication is ineffective. Off time can result from small daily changes, such as to diet, as well as the loss of dopamine neurons over time. Some of those treatments are moving into phase III trials for efficacy. More trials are in the works, raising cautious hopes that a new treatment for the disease is on the horizon. One of the first trials to test the cells in people with Parkinson’s was successful enough that the treatment is already available in Japan, albeit under strict regulatory oversight.

“This is such an exciting place to be,” says Claire Henchcliffe, a neurologist at the University of California, Irvine. “These are first-in-human trials. We’ve never had any products like these before.”

Despite the momentum, no one thinks that the treatment is ready for large-scale use. The trials so far have been small, with no control groups, and were designed to measure safety, not effectiveness. They’ve opened up a host of questions for researchers to investigate, including which type of cell to transplant, how many to deliver and where to inject them. There’s also work to be done to understand how the brain responds to its new members.

Transplanting foreign cells requires around one year of immunosuppression, and the brain surgery itself carries risks, including haemorrhage and infection. But the trials move cell transplants from a theory requiring proof to an early-stage treatment needing development, says molecular neurobiologist Kwang-Soo Kim at McLean Hospital in Belmont, Massachusetts, who completed the first transplant of neurons derived from the cells of a person with Parkinson’s in 20171. The question now, Kim says, is, “How can we optimize them?”

To begin down the road to approval, researchers led by Jun Takahashi at Kyoto University, Japan, injected cells grown from donor tissue — known as allogenic cells — into the brains of seven people with Parkinson’s. The procedure seemed to be safe: none developed tumours, a concern of transferring immature cells into the body2.

Positron emission tomography (PET) scans showed that, two years after surgery and around 9 months after immunosuppression was stopped, on average, participants had more dopamine in the putamen — the part of the brain into which the neurons are injected — than they did before the procedure. This showed that the transplanted cells remained biologically active, even after immunosuppression was stopped. The movement symptoms of some of the participants also showed signs of improvement.

On the basis of the results, the Japanese government gave the team conditional approval for the cell transplantations. This regulatory stage gives people access to the therapy, and the costs are covered by the national health insurance system, while researchers closely observe and document their progress — similar to being in a phase III clinical trial in the United States. Full approval will take seven years, Takahashi says, during which his team will monitor safety and efficacy.

The concept behind stem-cell therapy for Parkinson’s was first tested in people in the 1980s, when researchers transplanted dopaminergic neurons taken from 8–10-week-old aborted fetuses into the brains of people with Parkinson’s. The participants showed improvements in their motor symptoms. After three years, one participant had improved enough to stop taking levodopa. Nearly two decades after treatment, two individuals still had the motor improvements seen in the years immediately after surgery and had stopped taking medication more than a decade earlier.

Dopamine neurons are lost in Parkinson’s.Credit: Janko Kajtez/Parmar lab

But this approach has a major flaw: fetal tissue is rare and difficult to obtain, and using cells derived from it in research is legally and ethically complex, says Malin Parmar, a neurobiologist at Lund University in Sweden. Parmar has worked on the TransEuro study, which used fetal tissue for the treatment of Parkinson’s3. “You can never upscale them into reliable therapies,” Parmar says.

But a 2006 discovery4 of how to revert any mature tissue into stem cells — dubbed induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) — and then coax them into becoming any other cell was a game-changer. Suddenly it was possible to imagine creating vast amounts of cells for research and medicine, and it didn’t take long for researchers to start probing the best ways to turn iPSCs into dopaminergic neurons — work that is now making its way to people. “It has turned from, ‘This has been done before, it won’t work,” to suddenly, ‘Oh boy, I can’t keep up with all the clinical trials,” Henchcliffe says.

In 2023, the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) cleared the way for Sumitomo Pharma in Osaka, Japan, which makes the cell product used by Takahashi, to conduct trials in the United States. Three people have already received transplants, says Joseph Ciacci, a neurosurgeon at the University of California, San Diego, who is leading the trial. His team aims to treat eight people.

Ciacci is hopeful that the brains of people he has treated can recover lost function after the transplants. The new neurons could be a buffer against treatments such as levodopa becoming less effective over time. “I feel very excited about it,” he says.

Sumitomo says it has also begun a larger trial that will enrol dozens of people, including a control group that will receive sham surgery. The company aims to compare the cells used in both trials and launch its therapy in the United States by 2032.

Three other trials have reported results so far, using a mix of cell types. All have a small sample size — fewer than 15 people — and none of them has a control group. The results should therefore be interpreted cautiously, researchers say. Still, all of the studies that have reported data met their safety endpoints and showed early signs of clinical benefit.

A trial involving 12 people, co-led by Henchcliffe, reported similar results to those of Takahashi’s team, including increased dopamine uptake at 18 months measured using PET and improvements in motor scores5. The trial was sponsored by stem-cell specialist BlueRock Therapeutics in Cambridge, Massachusetts, which is a subsidiary of multinational pharmaceutical company Bayer.

Blue Rock’s cell product, called bemdaneprocel, received the FDA’s Regenerative Medicine Advanced Therapy (RMAT) designation in 2024 and the Japanese health ministry’s Pioneering Regenerative Medical Product designation in December 2025. The team is currently enrolling participants in a phase III trial that will include a sham-surgery control group; it aims to transplant cells into 102 people in the United States, Canada and Australia and monitor their motor function for 18 months.

A third trial in eight individuals, run by the biotech company Aspen Neuroscience in San Diego, California, used dopaminergic neurons generated from the participants’ own cells, known as autologous cells. The cell recipients showed motor improvements, and several were able to reduce their dose of levodopa, according to results presented at the International Conference on Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s Diseases in March.

Dopaminergic progenitor cells are injected into the brain of a person with Parkinson’s.Credit: Kyoto University Hospital

The company has now completed transplants in another seven people with its cell product, called sasineprocel, and received RMAT designation in July. It plans to begin a phase III trial of the treatment this year.

In the same month, Parmar and her colleagues reported the first results of a trial, called STEM-PD, in which they transplanted neurons derived from embryonic stem cells into eight patients. The participants showed “good early signs” of symptom improvement, Parmar says. Six of the seven people who completed the follow-up period opted to reduce their dose of levodopa as a result. Similar to the other trials, none grew tumours or had other serious reactions to the cells, but one participant died ten weeks after the transplant owing to an infection they developed while taking immunosuppressive drugs6.

Taken together, Parmar says, the trial results show that the transplanted cells survive and don’t generate tumours. But more people need to be followed up for longer periods before the treatment can truly be called effective, especially given that treatments such as levodopa already exist, she says. She recommends that researchers adopt an approach of skynda långsamt, a Swedish phrase meaning to rush slowly. “What we have is really hopeful and very promising,” Parmar says. “But the expectations are super high.”

While trials seek evidence that the approach works, researchers are also trying to get a better understanding of how the brain responds to allogeneic and autologous transplants, with an eye to further boosting safety and efficacy.

Allogenic transplants require that people undergo immunosuppression, generally for one year, to prevent the brain from attacking or rejecting the cells. But some researchers are working on a way to do away with that need by genetically ‘cloaking’ allogenic cells — editing certain genes to hide the cells from the immune system7.

Last year, a team led by researchers at the Florey Institute in Melbourne, Australia, coaxed human stem cells into overexpressing genes that modulate the immune system. They then grew the cells into neurons and implanted them into a rat model of Parkinson’s. The rats that received the edited cells mounted less of an immune response than did those that received unedited neurons, and showed greater improvement in motor symptoms8.

Autologous cells don’t require such immunosuppression. But they do have their own drawbacks. Because they need to be generated for each person, individuals need to wait months before the cells can be implanted — a particular problem for people with Parkinson’s, whose neurons are continuously being destroyed. Using individualized cells for each transplant also introduces variation that makes measuring outcomes in clinical trials difficult, Parmar says. It’s more expensive than a treatment using allogenic cells, too, which researchers hope will eventually be available in large, off-the-shelf batches.

It’s even possible, says Parmar, that autologous cells from a person with Parkinson’s might be innately susceptible to developing the disease after transplantation, meaning that the treatment’s success could be shorter-lived. In 2020, Parmar and her team transplanted neurons derived from either an embryonic stem-cell line or a person with a gene mutation linked to Parkinson’s into a rat model of the disease. Both types of cell survived and rats receiving either type had improved symptoms. But in the rats that received the cells with the Parkinson’s gene, the transplanted grafts showed early signs of disease development9. Regardless of the source, turning immature brain cells into a viable, accessible treatment will require improvements to the processes for generating them en masse. Researchers are hoping that automation and standardization will bring down both the cost and the time needed to produce them. Some draw comparisons to full-genome sequencing: the first full human genome cost hundreds of millions of dollars to sequence, but today it can be done for about US$1,000.

Work is also needed to improve the survival of implanted cells. Although the trials — which are testing both high and low cell doses — show that some cells do take root in the brain and become productive dopamine-producing neurons, many more do not. In the BlueRock trial, for example, researchers delivered 900,000 cells to each side of the brain of people in the low-dose group, but they expected that only 150,000 cells per side would survive. In the high-dose group, participants received 2.7 million cells on each side of the brain in an attempt to have 300,000 survive5.

“After the cells are put into brain, you have no more control,” says Su-Chun Zhang, director of the Center for Neurologic Diseases at Sanford Burnham Prebys, a non-profit research institute in La Jolla, California. “They are on their own.”

Some researchers who are trying to improve cell survival think that the environment into which cells are transplanted might matter — just as the quality of a plot of land can affect a gardener’s outcomes. “We have spent many, many years to improve the seed,” Kim says. “But we didn’t pay attention to the soil.”

Like fertilizing soil, preparing the brain before the transplant could help. Some groups, for example, are exploring whether injecting specific growth factors along with the cells might coax them into becoming mature dopamine neurons. And in 2023, Kim and his team discovered a phenomenon they called ‘needle trauma’ in mice, in which the brain responds to placebo injections with an immune response that causes inflammation and kills brain cells. Transplanting immune cells called T cells along with the placebo injection suppressed the response10.

Kim is also concerned about the potential for cells to acquire mutations during the reprogramming and manufacturing process — and the potential long-term effects of such genetic changes, given that the cells might remain in a person’s brain for decades. “Stem-cell therapies are living products,” Kim says. Questions about such genomic integrity highlight the careful balance researchers must strike when pursuing a desperately sought after and potentially life-changing treatment but one that researchers still know so little about. That was obvious to Kim in 2020, when he was inundated with calls, e-mails and letters from people with Parkinson’s and their families after the publication of preliminary results for the first person to receive his transplant.

“We have to keep optimistic, and we have to give them hope,” Kim says. “But very informed hope.”

Mikel Arteta has praised Noni Madueke’s response to a difficult start to the season after the winger played another decisive role in Arsenal’s 1-0 victory over Hull City.

Martin Odegaard scored the only goal at the Emirates Stadium after 72 minutes, reacting quickest when Kostas Tzolakis saved Madueke’s effort.

Arsenal were far from their fluent best, but the victory moved the defending champions six points clear at the top of the Premier League.

As reported by Arsenal News, Arteta believes Madueke has transformed his performances after responding positively to limited playing time earlier in the campaign.

Arteta said of Madueke: “That’s the second part of the story – the first is that you need to earn the right to be able to do that.

“Noni did that, he reacted to not playing often, went away, started to train and was a different Noni.

“He wasn’t going to accept that situation, he meant business, and since then he has been incredible.

“Now you are in that position, he needs to hone and improve it, so let’s see if he can do that.”

Madueke was Arsenal’s most dangerous attacker against Hull, registering five successful dribbles and creating several opportunities.

Sky Sports also reports that he is now averaging 3.57 chances created per 90 minutes, the highest rate of any Premier League player this season.

Madueke’s improvement could be particularly important while Bukayo Saka is unavailable.

Earlier in the season, a January exit was even being discussed. CaughtOffside reported in September that Atletico Madrid and Juventus were monitoring his situation after his limited Premier League involvement.

That possibility now feels considerably less likely.

Madueke has responded exactly how Arteta would have wanted: rather than becoming frustrated, he worked independently during the international break and returned sharper. His passing accuracy, crossing and dribble success have all improved compared with last season.

There is still one obvious area to improve. Madueke had chances to score against Hull and could have made the victory far more comfortable.

But Arsenal now have a winger who is creating chances at an elite rate and increasingly influencing important matches. If he can add more ruthless finishing, Arteta may soon face a genuine selection dilemma when Saka returns.

Right, where were we? Three weeks on from the fifth round of Premier League fixtures in which the champions Arsenal were beaten 3-0 by Brighton and todays’ visitors, Leeds United, who remain unbeaten, drew in a tepid goalless fixture with Crystal Palace, we finally get to the sixth. As worrying as the result was at the Amex, Arsenal still created a shedload of chances and last season they were the one club that battered Leeds in both games – first early in the season when they were playing four at the back and before Dominic Calvert-Lewin, a late signing, was fully fit, and then later after they had successfully switched to a “base formation” of three centre-backs and the tactical flexibility that allowed.

It was a 5-0 tanking in August and 4-0 in January, so to say Leeds travel to a ground at which they have never won more in hope than expectation would be as true as much as it is hackneyed. Adding to a sense of foreboding and thanks to Opta’s excellent Jonny Cooper, we also have to take into account the fact that Leeds, floodlight kings, have not won a Premier League match kicking off before 3pm since August 2022 and have not won a match in London since beating Brentford in May that year to save themselves from relegation. However, they do boast the division’s best defensive record – three goals conceded – and the No1 ranked goalkeeper in James Trafford who has a save percentage of 87. For all the sense of doom, though, Leeds have become a very good side and their spine – Trafford–Muharemovic–Ampadu–Calvert-Lewin marries steel and class.

Arsenall need no fanfare. Until the set-back in dear old Sussex by the sea, they had looked formidable most of the time and will have been champing at the bit to get back out there and prove it was an aberration. Mikel Arteta mentioned he has doubts about Declan Rice, Kai Havertz and Ezri Konsa but Ben White, Max Dowman and Chrsthian Mosquera are all available. For Leeds Joe Rodon is still out and Dan James was injured on international duty but Harry Wilson and Jean-Matteo Bahoya returned to training after knocks this week and Daniel Farke was relatively optimistic about their prospects.

#1331. Could chemicals contribute to Parkinson’s?

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Tammy Worth is a freelance health-care reporter in Kansas City, Missouri.

Potential links between pesticide exposure and health problems are hard to tease out.Credit: brt COMM/Alamy

In May, Vermont became the first US state to pass legislation that bans most uses of paraquat, a chemical herbicide linked to an increased risk of Parkinson’s disease. Other states have also examined paraquat’s safety. California’s Department of Pesticide Regulation studied the chemical in 2024, but chose not to ban it. However, in August, after persistent advocacy from farm workers and environmental groups, the state announced plans to phase out paraquat over a two-year period.

Paraquat is already banned in 70 countries, including China, Brazil, Turkey and member states of the European Union (where it’s been prohibited for nearly 20 years). And paraquat isn’t the only chemical under scrutiny. Other pesticides have been identified as potential triggers of Parkinson’s disease, including the heavy metals; the fish poison rotenone and the solvent trichloroethylene (TCE), which used in dry cleaning.

Although many researchers are certain that environmental factors play a fundamental part in Parkinson’s risk, they have struggled to convince regulators, particularly at the US federal level. Population studies take decades to complete, and the interplay between environmental toxicants and individuals’ genetic risk is difficult to tease out. But many neurologists and Parkinson’s advocates think that the science is sufficient to link some chemicals to the condition.

The delay in regulatory action is not caused by a lack of research, says Beate Ritz, an epidemiologist at the Fielding School of Public Health at the University of California, Los Angeles. “You can pile on as much science as you want to; it won’t change a thing until there is political will.”

It’s widely accepted that Parkinson’s disease is linked to a combination of factors, including genetics, changes to the brain as it ages and environmental triggers.

Genetics might be the most well-understood factor. About 20 gene variants have been linked to Parkinson’s. These variants are thought to cause the accumulation of proteins that clump to form Lewy bodies — aggregations that damage dopamine-producing nerve cells and deplete the brain’s supply of this ‘feel-good’ neurotransmitter. The loss of dopamine affects the brain’s ability to control movement.

But genetics accounts for only about 5–15% of cases of Parkinson’s disease. Other causes include behavioural factors such as physical activity, diet and smoking. Head trauma, some medications and even having red hair (because of a mutation in the MC1R gene) could also increase risk.

The potential link between chemicals and Parkinson’s was discovered in the early 1980s. Neurologist William Langston and his colleagues at the Santa Clara Valley Medical Center in San José, California, found that a small number of people who had taken a synthetic opioid called MPTP exhibited Parkinson’s-like symptoms1. Langston noted that when MPTP entered the brain, it was quickly converted to the toxic metabolite MPP+, which damages dopamine-producing neurons and is structurally similar to chemicals such as paraquat.

There’s seldom a one-to-one correlation between a toxicant and the development of Parkinson’s, says Rebecca Gilbert, a neurologist specializing in Parkinson’s disease and chief mission officer of the New York City-based American Parkinson Disease Association. She says it’s rare that someone’s Parkinson’s can be traced directly to them playing on their grandfather’s farm that was sprayed with paraquat when they were seven years old. Instead, it’s typically an amalgam of several risk factors. “I picture it like a glass of water,” Gilbert says. “You pour in that exposure to the spraying when you were seven, and then you pour in genetics, and then you pour in a little TCE.”

Part of the challenge of deciphering how different chemicals contribute to Parkinson’s disease is that much of the damage occurs slowly, long before a person is diagnosed. And during those years, other factors can modify disease progression — making it difficult to pinpoint which exposures matter.

Study participants can’t be exposed to pollutants deliberately, so scientists seeking to establish that association are left with epidemiological and animal studies. But epidemiological studies take decades, and no country has an official registry of people with Parkinson’s disease for researchers to contact. And animal studies can’t completely mimic either the age-related loss of dopamine-producing brain cells or the full range of Parkinson’s symptoms.

Ray Dorsey, a neurologist at the Atria Health and Research Institute in New York City, studies environmental triggers of Parkinson’s. In work published in 2023, he highlighted a handful of case studies of people who developed Parkinson’s after TCE exposure2. One of these looked at 99 pairs of twins and found that exposure to TCE increased the risk of Parkinson’s by more than 500%. “We’re paying a really high price for dry-cleaning things,” Dorsey says.

One of the most well-known epidemiological studies of Parkinson’s involved military personnel stationed at Camp Lejeune, North Carolina. In 1982, the US Marine Corps found that water on the base was contaminated with volatile organic compounds, most notably TCE. A study3 published in 2023 focused on the health conditions of people who had been at Camp Lejeune for at least three months between 1975 and 1985. When researchers followed up these individuals between 1997 and 2021, they found that their rate of Parkinson’s disease was 70% higher than it was among personnel who had been living at Camp Pendelton, California — where the water was not contaminated — for at least three months during that same ten-year period3. Even among the Camp Lejeune veterans who did not have Parkinson’s, there was a higher prevalence of symptoms that might pre-date a Parkinson’s diagnosis, such as constipation, tremors and loss of sense of smell.

Use of the weedkiller paraquat has been linked to Parkinson’s disease.Credit: Romeo Gacad/AFP via Getty

Ritz uses geographical information system modelling to track environmental exposures and their link to conditions such as Parkinson’s. One of her focuses is farming communities. In a study published in 2024, she and her colleagues analysed people living or working near three agricultural counties in central California where farms were treated with paraquat4. The data went back to 1974, and peoples’ exposure times ranged from about 8 to 30 years. The researchers found that having higher exposure at work or at home increased the chance of getting Parkinson’s by 91%.

It’s intuitive to study people living and working in farming communities because of their direct contact with chemicals and the ability to track which products are used. But Dorsey co-authored a 2025 paper that found that the risk could extend to a wider population5. The study tracked people living near golf courses in Minnesota and Wisconsin. The researchers compared a 5,113-person control group and 419 people with Parkinson’s and found that living within 1.6 kilometres of a golf course raised the chance of getting Parkinson’s by 126%, compared with the risk for people who lived at least 9.6 kilometres away. The researchers also observed that this risk dropped the farther away people lived. The authors posited that the increased risk close by could be due to exposure to pesticides through inhalation and groundwater. Researchers didn’t measure the types or levels of pesticides, but noted that they are frequently used on golf courses, particularly in the United States, which uses as much as 15 times more pesticides on golf courses than do European countries.

“It shouldn’t be terribly surprising,” Dorsey says, “that chemicals designed to damage the nervous system of insects might have similar consequences on the nervous system of humans.”

Rotenone is another pesticide that could contribute to Parkinson’s. But there are few human studies that link it to the condition. One commonly cited study from 2011 compared 110 people with Parkinson’s (mostly farmers) who had formerly applied restricted-use pesticides on private property and a control group of 358 people from Iowa and North Carolina who regularly used chemicals at work in the 1990s, but were not cognitively impaired or diagnosed with Parkinson’s. Researchers found that people who had worked with rotenone — which degrades the function of mitochondria — had a 2.5 times higher risk of developing Parkinson’s than did people in the control group6. More-recent animal studies lend credence to this link. A 2025 study found that rats exposed to rotenone for 21 days had dysfunction in motor cortex synapses and upregulation of C1q (a glycoprotein) in the substantia nigra, a part of the brain that is affected in Parkinson’s7. This increased activity suggests an inflammatory response in that region of the brain.

For Parkinson’s researchers, chemicals linked to the condition can’t be banned quickly enough. But regulators in the United States seem more hesitant than their counterparts in many other countries.

The European Union banned TCE a decade ago. The US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) released a review of TCE in 2024 that prohibited its use in consumer products and many industrial and commercial products as of 15 September 2025. There are exceptions for some applications, however, including one lasting 50 years for what the EPA calls “essential laboratory use”.

Paraquat is undergoing review by the EPA, in a process conducted on regulated pesticides at least every 15 years. The agency has requested more data from manufacturers, and has said that it will host a roundtable to solicit public input.

Rotenone is banned in the European Union and the United Kingdom, but continues to be used in the United States and Canada to control invasive fish populations.

“The EPA demands an absurd level of proof that something is dangerous,” says Tim Greenamyre, a neurologist at the University of Pittsburgh in Pennsylvania. “They don’t like epidemiological studies,” he says, but they also “throw out animal studies because they say toxicants aren’t given at the exact dose that humans get”.

Greenamyre has a personal stake in this issue. He studied rotenone in his lab for decades and was himself diagnosed with Parkinson’s in 2021. Because of the lack of research on chemical causes of the disease, he says, any connection between his exposure and his diagnosis would only be speculative. But he hopes to help fill that gap in knowledge: he has received funding to study the mechanism by which rotenone, TCE and paraquat might trigger Parkinson’s.

Another open question is how many other chemicals might cause damage to the brain similar to that in Parkinson’s. Ritz’s current research is focusing on organophosphates and organochlorides, but she says there are many other potential offenders, including carbamates, pyrethroids and neonicotinoids — all pesticides.

Researchers such as Ritz have access to pesticide report systems that record who is spraying which chemical, where and when. But by the time they finish studying one pesticide, it has been replaced with a different one, which is later replaced by yet another.

“We are basically 20–30 years behind what’s happening in the fields,” Ritz says. And with every new contaminant that enters the scene, the potential that one might trigger Parkinson’s ticks up a notch.

#1329. New mum and ex-Lionesses star Mary Earps names baby boy Xander after announcing her partner's secret birth in heartwarming Instagram video

Published: 04:55 EDT, 8 November 2026 | Updated: 05:11 EDT, 8 November 2026

Euro-winning Lionesses goalkeeper Mary Earps has named her son Xander after becoming a mother for the first time, having revealed this week that her partner has given birth to a baby boy.

Earps, 33, was a hero of England's Euro 2022 victory at Wembley and starred at the World Cup in 2023, saving a penalty in the final. She won BBC Sports Personality of the Year but later lost her England place to rival Hannah Hampton and retired in acrimonious circumstances.

She moved to France with Paris Saint-Germain but returned to England earlier this year - and has now welcomed her first child with her partner, Kitty Forrest.

'Welcome to the world, Xander,' she posted on Instagram, with a photograph of her newborn's hand.

In a video released on Friday, Earps said: 'I've been keeping a little secret from you all. And I don't think I can talk my way out of this one. So, I think I'm going to have to show you.

'I can't quite believe I'm writing this, but yesterday Kitty and I welcomed our beautiful baby boy into the world!

'We're absolutely over the moon and still trying to take it all in. It's been such an emotional journey getting to this point, and we couldn't be more excited to start this next chapter of our lives as a family of three.'

Mary Earps has revealed the name of her baby boy following his secret birth: Xander

Earps and her partner Kitty (second right) revealed news of welcoming a baby boy (YouTube/Mary Earps)

Earps says she will not be able to take maternity leave due to the rigors of the football season. Her team, London City Lionesses, are eight games into the new Women's Super League season and sit third behind Chelsea and Manchester City.

'I do have one eye sort of on football, which is super weird,' she said.

'In any other job, you would just be like, "Okay, bye. Taking maternity leave, whatever. Um, and you just do what you need to do." But that doesn't really work in football, because you've got games and then, if you take the day off, then you got to think about what that looks like and how that works into sort of your training schedule and the fixture calendar.

'So, it's a little bit more complicated. You can't just take annual leave whenever you want without consequence. You know, it's going to be interesting to see what the next days and weeks bring.'

Earps first revealed that she was in a same-sex relationship in September of last year but largely kept partner Kitty out of the spotlight.

Kitty is a physiotherapist who worked as the lead in her department at Manchester United Women, Earps's former club.

Earps is pictured kissing the trophy after England won Euro 2022 at Wembley Stadium

Earps won BBC Sports Personality of the Year in 2023 following her Euro heroics

In a statement at the time, Earps said: 'I've always tried to keep my personal life separate from my professional one, but it would have felt inauthentic not to include something so important to me in this book. I'm in a really happy relationship.

'The people closest to me have always known, and I feel ready and happy to share that with everyone else now.'

Earps retired from England duty in May last year after the release of her autobiography dragged up a storm with Hampton, the Chelsea goalkeeper who overtook her from understudy to become England No 1.

Earps revealed she told Sarina Wiegman that 'bad behaviour was being rewarded' after Hampton was recalled to the England squad.

#1328. Man Utd make worst start in 40 years after being hauled back by 10-man Spurs

Manchester United fans were never going to pass up the opportunity to aim a volley of abuse in the direction of their bitter rivals.

By the end of another deeply unconvincing performance, though, they were more preoccupied by the problems afflicting their own team than the cheating scandal engulfing Manchester City.

Against City at Old Trafford last month, United lost to a team who were down to 10 men after just 23 minutes.

This time around they could not hold on to a lead against a Tottenham Hotspur side also navigating a numerical disadvantage following Rodrigo Bentancur’s sending off.

Rodrigo Bentancur dives in on Luke Shaw and it's all kicking off at Old Trafford! 🫨 https://t.co/uJUAMuZNzc

The sum total of it all is that United have now made their worst start to a season for 40 years, which is saying something given the traumas of the post-Ferguson era, and perhaps more disconcertingly, look to all intents and purposes like a team going backwards.

The bounce they enjoyed under Michael Carrick last season en route to Champions League qualification is over and, after just six points from as many games, it is hard to shake the feeling that it is going to be anything but a serious battle to finish in the top four or five.

The supporters did not hide their disgruntlement. There were boos around the half hour mark after an insipid opening when Spurs did everything but score and a slow, sluggish, dishevelled United almost looked impervious to their troubles.

Carrick had called for his players to show some “fire” coming into this match, but instead watched them ambling around like it was all a terrible inconvenience. The ease with which Spurs ran around them was alarming. There were more jeers at the interval and again at full time.

Carrick admitted that “hurt” although not as much you suspect as the sight of players feigning interest and then throwing away three points when they had finally summoned some fight to lead courtesy of Bryan Mbeumo’s goal.

Bryan Mbeumo slots it home to give Manchester United the lead against Spurs! 🎯 https://t.co/7yKnpyhfUe

It was a lovely finish after good work by the largely anonymous Matheus Cunha, and when Bentancur was sent off five minutes later after butting Luke Shaw, it should have been the cue to see out the game. To fail to do so against a side as toothless as Tottenham made it all the worse. Leading late on against Everton last month, they also failed to get over the line. It cannot keep happening.

Equally, United cannot play like they did in the first half here when they face Atlético Madrid in the Spanish capital on Tuesday night or at Elland Road against bitter rivals Leeds five days later and expect to get anything from either game. They are not the sort of matches Carrick would want with his team in this shape, but they need to find some inspiration from somewhere.

Carlos Baleba coming on around the hour mark and making a difference on his debut will at least offer Carrick some grounds for encouragement. The £65m midfield signing from Brighton offers some energy and urgency and looks a more natural bedfellow for Kobbie Mainoo than Youri Tielemans, who was woeful against Spurs and should have come off earlier.

In truth, Tielemans was not alone. Throughout the team there was a disconnect and unease and Carrick admitted it became contagious.

“We just couldn’t find a way to get ourselves into the game, whether that was with the ball or without the ball,” the United manager said. “We were a little bit slow with the decision-making, didn’t quite see the passing areas, the space. You don’t want it to happen, but sometimes it can and it probably spread through the team a little bit too much.”

It does not help that Bruno Fernandes is being hampered by an injury he has been carrying for weeks or that Carrick has no natural centre-forward to call upon with Benjamin Sesko again sidelined by the recurrence of a worrying shin problem. Amad Diallo did return here after a lengthy lay-off of his own, but did not look match fit.

In defence, Lisandro Martínez did enough to put off Dominic Solanke, who fired over from Sávio’s cross in the second half, but this was otherwise another poor showing from the Argentine centre-back, one of several positions where United need upgrades.

United needed shaking badly, but when Carrick turned to his bench he called upon Joshua Zirkzee, a fitful forward the club wanted to sell this summer, and right-back Diogo Dalot in addition to Baleba.

Marcus Rashford cannot have been fit given he was only introduced in the 95th minute and perhaps the same was true of the unused Mason Mount. As for £50m summer signing Andrey Santos, this was another league game when the Brazilian midfielder did not get a look in.

United fans had taunted Spurs when a goal and a man up. “You’re going down with the City,” they crowed, a nod to the possibility of City being expelled or relegated from the Premier League after being found guilty of breaching more than 100 financial rules.

United fans had also revived their Stretford End “ticker” after reaching the conclusion that none of City’s titles under Abu Dhabi ownership had been won fairly so, in their eyes, it is now 50 years since their rivals last won anything legitimately. City, of course, continue to maintain their innocence and have lodged an appeal.

But United fans were unable to crow for too long once Solanke levelled.

Spurs are level in stoppage-time! 😳 https://t.co/NoivNchgWw

It had been similar early in the game when the home fans had trained their sights on City. “You cheating b--------, you know what you are”, they sang lustily.

But as the match wore on, those chants began to quieten as the crowd, taking their lead from the team, fell decidedly flat.

Carrick is going to have to find a spark from somewhere and quickly.

Speaking to BBC Match of the Day, Carrick said: “It was a mixed game. We found it tough to start with. For a number of reasons, we were not quite there. You could see it was a challenging time.

“But the lads grew into the game, in the second half I thought we were better in everything. To get the game as we wanted it, in such a good position - we should see it through. We have to manage those situations. That’s two late goals which have hurt us, and things look very different. That’s the reality.”

When asked about the boos at half-time and full-time, he replied: “It’s not nice, it hurts a lot because I care about this club. But I understand the disappointment, the reality is what it is, we need to get back to winning games.”

3 - Manchester United have failed to win any of their last three Premier League games against sides that have received a red card (D1 L2). Disadvantage? https://t.co/DuSpvymZfu

The Tottenham boss told Sky Sports: “I think we played very well against a great team. We had many chances to score in the first half. Three or four. The second half is normal to suffer against this quality. I am very happy because I have seen the right spirit and character.

“We suffered in the game but every situation of the game. I like the situation we were in with the red card. We need this situation. We have not accepted the defeat. We have to react in all ways we can. It is a bad way, it is not the right way. I kiss Bentancur in the dressing room. Football is character.

“We win the game if we play as a team. We didn’t win this game playing as a team. Every game like today, we will win many games.”

When asked about Solanke, he replied: “He is a good player for Tottenham. There for not too many strikers better than Solanke. Today he was captain because he deserved it, especially in this moment because he suffer because Tottenham didn’t score or win any games. He is a great guy, great player and we are behind him.

“We have to believe in ourselves and this football way. If we believe, improve and play as a team, we will score many goals and win many games. If we don’t play as a team, it is impossible.”

"Today we showed so much fight and grit!" Dominic Solanke on Spurs' mentality to rescue a point at Old Trafford 💪 https://t.co/jurK07E6jU

"They look devoid of any confidence" Jamie Redknapp says Manchester United's squad is not strong enough ❌ https://t.co/oZgmtWelJB

"They were the better team today by far" Gary Neville reacts at full-time as Spurs grab a late equaliser at Manchester United 💬 https://t.co/T37kkDy5uj

More jeers at the final whistle from United fans - they weren’t happy with this point against a team there for the taking after Rodrigo Bentancur’s dismissal. Michael Carrick is still trying to find answers because this United team is not clicking.

The late chaos is over at Old Trafford as Solanke rescues a precious point for Tottenham with that 92nd minute equaliser. Man Utd thought they had the game wrapped up after Mbeumo’s well-taken opener was followed by Bentancur’s crazy red card. However, Spurs, who were the better team throughout the contest, kept fighting and found a fully deserved leveller. The visitors remain winless, but it’s another worrying performance from Carrick’s side, who have picked up just one victory in six top-flight matches.

A point apiece in Manchester. https://t.co/xiEiQsFsje

Dalot and Gray are both handed yellow cards for fouls that broke up play. Despite their numerical disadvantage, Spurs currently look like the more likely side to claim a victory.

It’s just the Spurs fans singing in Old Trafford now. They fully deserved that equaliser. Rashford and Heaven are on for the hosts, with Cunha and Shaw taken off.

Incredible drama at Old Trafford! Tonali floats a cross into the box and Solanke shrugs off Martinez, before flicking a delicate header into the bottom corner to send Spurs’ away support wild. Man Utd are stunned. Could the visitors go on and win this now?

Spurs are level in stoppage-time! 😳 https://t.co/NoivNchgWw

Van Hecke does well to block Cunha’s effort and the referee indicates that there will be a minimum of eight minutes of added time.

De Zerbi’s final roll of the dice in search of a late leveller sees Fernandes replace Senesi for the remaining few minutes. Spurs must throw everyone forward now.

Martinez lunges in on Maddison and brings down the playmaker with a foul. The centre-back picks up a yellow card for his troubles.

Baleba unleashes Mbeumo with an over-the-top through ball. Racing through on goal, the forward shoots, but from an unfavourable angle, Kinsky parries his near post effort out for a corner.

Fernandes is cautioned after catching Van Hecke with a late challenge on his ankle. Spurs players aren’t happy with the tackle.

Bentancur’s recklessness has left Spurs with a mountain to climb. Their chance of a comeback looks a bit slimmer now that Man Utd have a numerical advantage on the pitch.

It’s all kicked off at Old Trafford! Bentancur flies in with a risky challenge on Shaw. The Man Utd defender is furious with the tackle and the two players square up to each other. Shaw pushes Bentancur over and the midfielder responds by leaning into the Englishman, creating a headbutt-like action. Shaw and Van Hecke are also given yellows for their roles in that altercation.

Rodrigo Bentancur dives in on Luke Shaw and it's all kicking off at Old Trafford! 🫨 https://t.co/uJUAMuZNzc

Rodrigo Bentancur is sent off... and here's why ⬇️ https://t.co/3ahzz5iUbg

Van Hecke allows the forward to turn and Mbeumo slides a delightful effort into the far bottom corner. Old Trafford erupts in joy. Tottenham can’t believe it.

Bryan Mbeumo slots it home to give Manchester United the lead against Spurs! 🎯 https://t.co/7yKnpyhfUe

Tonali’s pass is intercepted by Maguire, but the ball trickles into the onrushing Savio’s path. The winger’s powerful first-time effort is blocked by Mainoo’s sliding challenge and flies over the bar.

It’s Tottenham’s turn to make some alterations as Bentancur and Marmoush enter the action, replacing Bergvall and Kudus.

Zirkzee turns Senesi and threads a pass through to Fernandes. From a tight angle, the Man Utd captain slices a ferocious effort into the side netting. The playmaker has been quiet today, but you can never write him off from scoring or providing an assist.

Baleba’s first action in a Man Utd shirt sees the midfielder smash a hopeful volley wildly off target. Can Baleba’s introductrion lift the crowd and help give the hosts some impetus?

Van Hecke wins the header at the back post of a corner, looping the ball right back into the danger zone, but Maguire is there to crucially nod it over the bar.

Man Utd have the ball in the net, but it won’t count, as Cunha failed to keep it in play before teeing up Tielemans to finish from close range. Old Trafford thought it had lift-off against the run of play, but they’ve been denied by the correct decision.

Tottenham will be kicking themselves! Once again, Savio is causing trouble for Man Utd, driving at the home side’s defence before crossing for Solanke.
